steps.text: thanks for being here. let's spend one minute on your side.
picture someone you love having a rough day. what would you want them to hear from you?

steps.prompt: pick any that fit, or none.
options: it makes sense this is hard
you don't have to be perfect
steps.reply: those are kind. now let's turn them toward you.

steps.prompt: say one to yourself, slowly, with your name. out loud if you can. tap the one you tried.
lines: {name}, it makes sense this is hard.
steps.reply: notice how that landed. that's the voice we're growing.

steps.text: compared to how you usually talk to yourself, how was that?

options.label: softer
options.reply: that softness is the whole point. it's yours, any time you want it.

options.label: strange
options.reply: of course. kind words to yourself can feel unfamiliar. they get easier with practice.

options.label: about the same
options.reply: that's okay too. sometimes it takes a few tries, and the right words.

steps.prompt: keep one kind line, in your own words:
ideas: don't have to be perfect to be okay.
are more than one hard day.

steps.text: being kind to yourself isn't going easy on yourself. across many studies, people who treat themselves kindly tend to report greater well-being.
steps.evidence: moderate (a consistent link across 79 samples; mostly not proof of cause)

steps.text: tonight, say your kind line to yourself once, using your name.

grounding.idea: self-compassion goes along with greater well-being
grounding.source: Zessin, Dickhäuser & Garbade, 2015, Applied Psychology: Health and Well-Being

grounding.idea: talking to yourself as "you" or by name reduces distress under stress
grounding.source: Kross et al., 2014, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
